11.24.12.en: In every case, praise of the dead is useful, first because, the person being absent, who will reward us for our praise of him? It is necessary that all the glory be referred to the Giver of grace. Second, admiration of virtue remains without doubt free from flattery. Therefore the praise of the dead that is proclaimed in the holy assembly of the believers is full of edification and free from any kind of flattery [24].

11.24.13.en: Hilary, bishop of Arles v "Boast not thyself of to morrow; for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth" (Prov 27:1). It is written: "Call no one blessed before his death." For as long as we live we are busy with a battle, and there is no sure victory such as appears in the life to come [25].

11.24.14.en: St. Jerome v How can you know him who is unknown even to himself?... Where then is the assurance? Here there is no assurance in this life, save only in hope of the promise of God. But there, when we arrive, we shall be in complete safety, where the doors are shut, where the bars of the gates of Jerusalem are strengthened (Ps 147:13). There is truly perfect exultation and great joy. You do not feel safe in praising any kind of life: "Call no one blessed before his death" (see Sir 11:26) [26].

11.24.15.en: St. Augustine v Death, which was hated, has become a subject of praise and is proclaimed as a blessed thing. What was at one time a cause of pain and sorrow and tears and gloom appears as a source of joy and festival. All the servants of God enjoy the blessed death, because the end of their life brings security where God welcomes them. In truth they become perfect, and this perfection restores to them their blessedness and gives them the firmness of virtue, as the teaching affirms: "Judge no one before his death" [26][27].

11.25.s.en: 7. True wisdom and caution against the wicked

11.25.0.en: 31 Do not bring every man into your house; for the schemes of the deceiver are many. 32 Like a decoy partridge in a cage, so is the heart of the proud, and he is like a spy watching for a fall. 33 For he lies in wait, turning good into evil, and stains the chosen with blemishes. 34 From one spark a fire is multiplied, and the sinful man lies in wait for blood. 35 Beware of the wicked man who devises evils, lest he bring upon you a disgrace forever. 36 Receive a stranger into your house, and he will upset your affairs with trouble, and drive you out of your own.

11.25.1.en: With Sirach's continual speaking about giving, almsgiving and love, he nevertheless wants the believer to keep to wisdom and moderation in every action for the edification of himself and of those with whom he deals. So he warns against the wicked exploiting the service given to strangers, the poor and enemies.

11.25.2.en: Ben Sira refuses giving to one who insists on evil, like one who takes alms to buy a weapon with which to kill, or to buy drugs, etc. [12:1-2]. Our Christ calls us in the Sermon on the Mount to give with love even to enemies (Mt 5:44-45), so that we bear witness to the love of God for sinners who have entered into enmity against God. St. Augustine sees that love moves us to give in the spirit of wisdom, so that if we know that the gift will be used to harm the one who asks alms or those around him, we ought to give him not money but, in a spirit of love and tenderness, offer him holy counsel in the Lord. In this we imitate the Lord, who even in His discipline offers love, with a longing for the wicked man to return from his wickedness.

11.25.3.en: Do not bring every man into your house, for the schemes of the deceiver are many [27].

11.25.4.en: It is fitting for the believer, with his love of hospitality to strangers, if a man is known to be a slanderer who spreads rumors and lies, not to invite him to his house, lest he spoil the purity of the hearts of the household. For the slanderer turns even good into evil, and by his false and lying words kindles a fire in the midst of the family whose consequences are not to be praised (Jas 3:5-6). The wicked man works to isolate his listener from his society, whether family (the household) or Church. St. Clement of Alexandria sees that he does not leave his house unguarded, hosting a deceitful man who may corrupt his purity and the purity of the members of his household [28].

11.25.5.en: v It is written: "Do not bring every man into your house" (see Sir 11:27). So when a stranger approaches you, first pray to God, and after that ask him about his concerns, where he came from and where he is going. If it appears to you that you ought to welcome him, receive him and ask him to depart after the meal, and do not give him anything else. For if you enter with him into material dealings beyond your capacity, you will not be able to bear him afterward [29].

11.25.6.en: St. Barsanuphius and his disciple John v I do not mean to diminish the virtue of our forefathers, especially hospitality. In truth it is among the loftiest virtues the fathers practiced, this which inclines toward piety. One of them received God the Savior at his table, and another received angels. One received a reward and had a son in his old age, and the other enjoyed salvation as he fled from Sodom (Gen 18-19). This is what the Apostle spoke of when he urged us to imitate him: "Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares" (Heb 13:2).

11.25.7.en: At any rate, let the person who offers hospitality have the wisdom of the serpent and the simplicity of the dove (Mt 10:16), obeying the Lord's double commandment: "Give to every man that asketh of thee" (Lk 6:30), "Do not bring every man into your house" [27]. This is so that you do not bring the danger of a wolf into a dwelling where a lamb lives (Mt 7:15), or a bear where there is an ox (Isa 11:7), which turns gain into loss.

11.25.8.en: First of all, it is necessary to take into account your ability to tolerate very difficult characters.

11.25.9.en: Finally you must consider who it is that you are receiving to obtain benefits from you, whether he is rich or poor, in good health or weak, in need of food or clothing. These are the fields in which mercy is practiced. In truth the blessed Abraham did not receive in his house (tent) counselors and leaders, the dominant persons of this passing world, who have horses... Abraham dwelt in an empty place receiving passers-by; those who travel in the desert came to the father, drawn toward his virtue, and some of them had become beggars in extreme poverty. In the same way Lot, who lived in the most wicked city in this desert, truly welcomed all passers-by, to preserve them from the customs of its inhabitants [30].

11.25.10.en: St. Palladius The heart of the proud is like a partridge set as a decoy in a cage, and like a spy watching for your fall [28].

11.25.11.en: It is stated in (Jeremiah 17:11): "The partridge utters its voice (the Septuagint), it gathers what it did not lay, he who gets riches unjustly; in the midst of his days he will leave them, and in his end he will be a fool." This was often a common proverb at that time, meaning that a man thinks he possesses, yet as he toils and labors he loses much, and wealth leaves him while he is still in the world in the midst of his days, but at his end he realizes that he walked in folly. This is the literal interpretation of the passage; and before we shed light on it through the deep spiritual meaning, we wish to clarify that the partridge is a wild bird, called in Hebrew "Qore," which means "the one who cries out or calls." And perhaps for this reason it came in the Septuagint version: "the partridge utters its voice" or "gives its voice"; it is one that has voices but no true work! So the rich man, in his bitter striving to enjoy wealth materially or to be satisfied bodily, is like one who gives a voice without work, for he leaves everything and goes out naked from this world.

11.25.12.en: St. Hippolytus sees that this bird is arrogant, for when the partridge sees the nest of another partridge with young ones without their mother, it makes a sound imitating the mother's voice and calls the young ones to it, and takes them and runs off with them. And it rejoices proudly that it has seized them, but when the true mother comes and calls with her voice, the young ones discover the deception of the first, and leave the deceiver and go to the true mother. This will happen when the Antichrist comes, for he draws humanity to himself by deception to reign over those who are not his, and promises them salvation though he is unable to save himself [31].

11.25.13.en: The partridge signifies the devil and his hosts, especially the heretics; it gives its own voice, and does not utter what belongs to God, while the children of God utter what belongs to God and not what belongs to themselves, as the Apostle Paul says: "Since ye seek a proof of Christ speaking in me" (2 Cor 13:3).

11.26.0.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa speaks of the man who is bound to the wiles of the devil and falls under the deceptions of the enemy: [The true good God and Father is no longer God and Father to him who by his corruption becomes an outlaw... and in place of the Father comes one who seems to be a father, who is falsely called the partridge that gathers what it did not lay, as Jeremiah says [32].]

11.26.1.en: Origen sees that Satan is the partridge, like Pharaoh who did not want the people to leave his land to worship the Lord.

11.26.2.en: For he lies in wait, and turns good into evil, and in the best of things finds fault with what the good man chooses [29].

11.26.3.en: From one spark a fire is kindled in the coals, and the sinful man lies in wait to shed blood [30].

11.26.4.en: Beware of the wicked man and his schemes, lest disgrace overtake you forever [31].

11.27.0.en: v Just as the simple and unlearned mock the sciences and refuse to listen to anything of them, because knowledge to them is folly, and so they wish that all should be ignorant like them, so also those who are dissolute in their life and morals have a great longing that all should be worse than they, thinking that by this they find an excuse for themselves, since the wicked are many [33].

11.27.1.en: v The wise man, or he who has begun to reform himself, is alone he who deserves to be called a man... for this quality (incorrigibility) does not befit a man, and such a man must be shunned.

11.28.0.en: Those who are pleased with iniquity will have no portion among the immortals [34].

11.28.1.en: St. Anthony the Great Receive a stranger into your house, and he will grieve you with troubles, and estrange from you the members of your household [32].

11.29.s.en: Grant me the spirit of love, management and security!

11.29.0.en: v Your divine presence sanctifies my family and my friends.

11.29.1.en: Often I relied on my human wisdom, and outward appearances deceived me in everyone I met.

11.29.2.en: Reveal Your presence within me, O You who are wonderful in Your humility!

11.29.3.en: In You I walk in the spirit of wisdom in humility.

11.29.4.en: Your wisdom carries me across from the last rows, and seats me in the council of the heavenly ones.

11.29.5.en: It removes from me the folly that brought me down to the dunghill.

11.29.6.en: v In You, O incarnate Wisdom of God, I am not deceived by a man's beauty and appearance.

11.29.7.en: And I mock no one because of a defect in his body!

11.29.8.en: The prophet Samuel looked at the beauty of Saul and his tall stature, and thought him the best fit to be king.

11.29.9.en: And You looked at the heart of the boy David, and prepared him to sit on the throne of Your people.

11.29.10.en: v Many look at the bee as a small insect that stings, and have not realized that many nations live on the honey it produces.

11.29.11.en: So many look at persons who seem to have no beauty, and do not realize that they will receive a glorious throne from Your hands.

11.29.12.en: A husband sometimes regrets that his wife lacks beauty of body, and has not realized that she surpasses many women in beauty of spirit and mind.

11.29.13.en: In his eyes she is a burden he wishes to be rid of, and in Your eyes her heart is a second heaven, rejoicing!

11.29.14.en: v Grant me prudence and not to be hasty in judging others.

11.29.15.en: Grant me not to cease from work until the last breath, imitating the angels who never tire of continual work according to Your will.

11.29.16.en: Grant me not to be troubled with many works, but to take care to be faithful in little, so that I may be made worthy to receive much in eternity.

11.29.17.en: Let me work with joy, and look forward to the day of my departure from the world rejoicing.

11.29.18.en: Grant me wisdom, that I may not allow everyone to enter my house, lest You, O Holy One, depart from it.

11.29.19.en: Grant me, in the midst of distress, not to desire failure for him who caused it to me.

11.29.20.en: Grant me, in the midst of my pains, to thank You for the former days of relief.

11.29.21.en: v In Your love You gave me free will; who can sanctify it and establish it except You?

11.29.22.en: In You I defy evil and embrace good; in You I thank You even if I become poor, and I serve You with what You have given me of possessions.

11.29.23.en: In You I defy death, and find sweet the life in You!

11.29.24.en: In the time of famine I do not forget the days of plenty, and in the time of prosperity I share with my brethren what You have given me!

11.29.25.en: v Let the days of my sojourn pass while I am in Your company, and let me look forward to death in the spirit of hope.

11.29.26.en: On the way of sojourn I neither criticize anyone nor praise him, for I look forward to Your grace with every morning.

11.29.27.en: Do not allow my heart, in my sojourn, to be proud.

11.29.28.en: Like the partridge shut up in a cage.

11.29.29.en: It does not cease its annoying cry without work!

11.29.30.en: Instead of this voice, let me enjoy Your sweet word.

11.29.31.en: For not by bread alone do I live here, but by every word that proceeds out of Your mouth.

11.29.32.en: Finally, sanctify me, O Holy One, and sanctify every family and all friends, indeed the whole world.

12.0.0.en: 1 If you do good, know to whom you do it, and your kindness will be acceptable. 2 Do good to the godly man and you will receive a reward; if not from him, then from the Most High. 3 There is no good for him who persists in evil and does not give alms, for the Most High hates sinners, and has mercy on the repentant. 4 Give to the godly man and do not help the sinner; for He will take vengeance on the hypocrites and sinners, but He keeps them for the day of vengeance. 5 Give to the good man, and do not support the sinner. 6 Do good to the humble man, and do not give to the hypocrite. Hold back your bread and do not give it to him, lest he be strengthened by it against you, 7 and you meet with evil twice as much as all the good you did to him. For the Most High hates sinners, and repays the hypocrites with vengeance.

12.0.1.en: The Apostle Paul warns us against hosting people who may cause us, as well as others, spiritual troubles, saying: "For of this sort are they which creep into houses, and lead captive silly women laden with sins, led away with divers lusts" (2 Tim 3:6).

12.0.2.en: Ben Sira offers us practical counsels on doing good to others:

12.0.3.en: a. In the spirit of wisdom we must get to know those to whom we do good, so that we offer them what is for their edification and ours and the edification of others.

12.1.0.en: b. Since we see in the needy man who receives the kindness the Savior of the world Himself, we must therefore care the more for the godly or for those who long for a life of godliness. This is what the Apostle called us to by saying: "As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith" (Gal 6:10). In this we offer the gift to the Most High Himself [2]. And on the other hand, it is fitting for us, even in our material giving, to offer the food of the spirit in a spirit of love and humility.

12.2.0.en: c. Not to be deceived by appearance, for a person may seem humble for a time, but time reveals his depths [11].

12.2.1.en: d. To take care that the person does not use the kindness for evil to himself or to others [3-4].

12.2.2.en: e. We support the needy so that he may not fall into evil, and so that he may not misuse the tenderness of the giver, especially if begging has turned into the practice of tricks in society. For instead of enjoying the kindness his evils increase and multiply [5].

12.2.3.en: If you do good, know to whom you do it, and you will be thanked for your good works [1].

12.2.4.en: St. Ambrose sees that every kindness offered to a poor or needy person is counted as fellowship with the woman who poured the ointment on the feet of the Lord Christ (Lk 7:38).

12.2.5.en: v Christ died once and was buried once, and yet He wishes that the ointment be poured on His feet every day. Who are counted as the feet of Christ, on whom we pour the ointment, except those of whom He said: "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me." These are the two feet that the woman mentioned in the Gospel refreshed, and washed with her tears [1].

12.2.6.en: St. Ambrose Do good to the godly man, and you will receive a reward; if not from him, then from the Most High [2].

12.2.7.en: v It appears that mercy toward the poor is truly the pouring of oil on God's sacrifice, while the service offered to the saints adds the sweetness of incense [2].

12.2.8.en: Origen v When someone preaches and you serve him, you share his crowns. For even in wrestling it is not the victor alone who takes the crown, but his trainer shares it with him, and those present and all who prepared the wrestling ring. Those who truly lead and train him share his victory... If we serve the saints with a good heart we share their reward. This is what Christ also tells us: "Make to yourselves friends of the mammon of unrighteousness; that, when ye fail, they may receive you into everlasting habitations" (Lk 16:9) [3].

12.2.9.en: St. John Chrysostom v When the blessed Apostle Paul helped the brethren in the needs of his affliction he said that these good works are sacrifices to God... So when one has compassion on a poor man he lends to God, and when he gives to the little ones he gives God spiritual sacrifices of a sweet-smelling aroma [4].

12.2.10.en: The Martyr Cyprian Father Caesarius, bishop of Arles, sees that man needs alms, not only of money with which to acquire food for his stomach, but also of the word of God so that his mind may be satisfied with the food of the spirit. Let us offer alms from the word of God, and not wait for anyone to repay it to us, but the Lord Himself will repay it to us.

12.2.11.en: v Perhaps a man has no bread to offer as alms to the needy, but there remains what is greater, that a man should have a tongue able to give. For he who refreshes the mind to live forever with the food of the Word is greater than he who satisfies with earthly food the stomach of the body that dies.

12.2.12.en: Therefore, brethren, do not refrain from offering the alms of the word to your relatives. Paul says: "If we have sown unto you spiritual things, is it a great thing if we shall reap your carnal things?" (1 Cor 9:11). "Do good to the godly man, and you will receive a great reward; if not from him, then surely from God" (see Sir 12:2) [5].

12.2.13.en: Father Caesarius, bishop of Arles There is no kindness to him who persists in evil, or who does not give alms with joy [3].

12.2.14.en: v Alms are given, but with wisdom to the deserving, that we may receive a reward from the Most High.

12.2.15.en: And woe to those who assume a deceptive appearance, and those who are able to help themselves and ask from others, for he who has means and pretends with a deceptive appearance or asks because of laziness is condemned [6].

12.2.16.en: St. Clement of Alexandria v Give to everyone who asks of you without return (Lk 6:30). For the Father wants all to share in the blessings that we have. Blessed is he who gives according to the commandment, for he is blameless. Woe to him who receives without need. If one receives out of want he is counted blameless. But if he receives without want, he will give account of the reason and the purpose for which he received. He is cast into prison, and is questioned about his conduct, and does not come out from there till he has paid the uttermost farthing (Mt 5:26). But it is also said in this regard: Let your alms sweat in your hands [7], until you know to whom you give [8].

12.2.17.en: The Didache Give to the godly man, and do not help the sinner [4].

12.2.18.en: Perhaps someone asks: How can one fulfill the commandment: "Give to him that asketh thee" (Mt 5:42) and also: "If thine enemy hunger, feed him" (Rom 12:20); and at the same time: "Do not help the wicked (the sinner)" [4]?

12.2.19.en: v Let mercy be exercised toward the wicked, not as being wicked, that is, do not receive the wicked as wicked, do not receive him because you incline to his evil and approve it. For it is forbidden to give to the wicked... But how do we listen to the saying: "Give to him that asketh thee" (Mt 5:24), and also: "If thine enemy hunger, feed him" (Rom 12:20)? Perhaps there seems to be in this a kind of contradiction, but let us open to those who knock in the name of Christ, and the matter becomes clear to him who asks...

12.2.20.en: If a sinner asks me, I give him, not as being a sinner. When do you give to him as a sinner? When you give him what makes him a sinner, and you are pleased when you give him... Would that those who give to a man who fights with wild beasts would tell me why they give to him?.. When you give, give to him so as to put him to shame, not to boasting (in error) [9].

12.2.21.en: v It seems at the end of the passage that it condemns kindness, for it says: "Do not help the sinner." You must understand that "the sinner" here represents sin symbolically, so that what we cease to help is his sin [10].

12.2.22.en: St. Augustine v It is written: "Place your bread and your wine on the tomb of the righteous, and do not eat or drink of them with sinners" (Tob 4:18), and he who offers bread and wine to the wicked offers help to the wicked for the sake of their wickedness. There are some rich men who feed the clowns of the theater lavishly, while poor Christians starve. But he who offers bread to the ungodly because he is a human being, and not because he is ungodly, in truth feeds a righteous beggar and not a sinner, for he loves in him his human nature and not his sin [11].

12.2.24.en: Do good to the humble man, and do not give to the wicked.

12.2.25.en: Hold back his bread, and do not give it to him, lest he rule over you by it.

12.2.26.en: And you will reap from evil twice as much as all the good you did to him [5].

12.3.0.en: "Do good to the humble man." This commandment, as Pope Gregory (the Great) says, is directed to the rich who flatter the prodigal at their banquets, while the poor suffer from hunger [12]. It is fitting for us to give to the poor as human beings and not as sinners; and if we realize that he uses the gift for evil, we may not support him.

12.3.1.en: For the Most High also hates sinners, and repays the wicked with punishment [6].

12.3.2.en: The Lord punishes sinners who persist in their evils and do not return to Him in repentance.

12.3.3.en: Give to the good man, and do not help the sinner [7].

12.3.4.en: The work of the divine commandment is to raise man gradually, especially in the practice of love and giving and not attacking others. This is what St. John Chrysostom and St. Augustine and others made clear. To clarify this we present in a few lines the degrees of the ladder of love:

12.3.5.en: a. At the bottom man tends to attack others without cause, so some tribes would attack neighboring tribes merely to seize some of their possessions or to dominate them. As we observe, some children, before they learn to speak, tend to snatch what is in the hands of other children even though they make no use of what they snatch.

12.3.6.en: b. As man ascends the ladder of love, he does not attack his brother without cause, but if the brother attacks him he returns the attack with a doubled attack in order to discipline him so that he does not repeat it.

12.3.7.en: c. The Mosaic Law rejected the two former degrees, and permitted man, because of his human weakness, to control himself, so that he returns the attack only in equal measure: "Eye for eye, tooth for tooth."

12.3.8.en: d. The believer can rise higher, so that he returns the blow with less than it, merely for discipline and not for punishment.

12.3.9.en: e. What is higher is that a man forgives his brother for what he did against him.

12.3.10.en: f. The Lord Christ came and called us to the glory of the liberty of the children of God to return evil with good, and not merely for the believer to give up his right. It was not possible to reach the last degree before the coming of the Lord Christ and our receiving the grace of sonship to God. Therefore the commandments in the Old Testament came to do good to the godly man, and permitted him not to do good to the wicked.

12.3.11.en: The commandment forbade doing good to the sinner not out of hatred for him, but so that he might review himself and turn back from his evil, and seek the life of godliness. The Apostle wanted the believers to support their brethren to grow in the holy, godly life, for he says: "As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith" (Gal 6:10).

12.4.0.en: 8 A friend is not known in prosperity, nor is an enemy hidden in adversity. 9 In a man's prosperity his enemies are grieved, and in his adversity even his friend departs. 10 Never trust your enemy, for his wickedness is like the rust of copper. 11 Even if he is humble and walks with bowed head, take heed to yourself and beware of him; for you will be with him as one who has polished a mirror, and you will know that its cleanness from rust does not last. 12 Do not make him stand near you, lest he overthrow you and stand in your place. Do not seat him at your right hand, lest he covet your seat. And in the end you will understand my words and be pricked by my sayings. 13 Who will pity a charmer bitten by a serpent? Or who will have compassion on those who go near wild beasts?

12.4.1.en: In difficult circumstances we can sort out the sincere friend from the enemy disguised in the garment of friendship. With wisdom the believer discerns the true friend from the enemy who has sweetness on his lips while he plans his friend's descent into a pit. The enemy's eyes may shed tears as one who pities him, while within him lies a desire to shed his blood.

12.4.2.en: As Ben Sira offered practical counsels in the spirit of wisdom and godliness concerning doing good, here he offers counsels that the believer ought to observe in choosing a friend, and they are:

12.4.3.en: a. Distress sorts the friend from the enemy. The first, with all his heart and capabilities, wants to help, while the second shows in his features and conduct the spirit of enmity, such as leaving him and ignoring him in the midst of distress [8-9].

12.4.4.en: b. Not to be hasty in choosing a friend, until time reveals him and distinguishes him.

12.5.0.en: c. Not to be deceived by appearance, for a person may seem humble, but time reveals his arrogant depths [11].

12.6.0.en: d. Not to give him the opportunity to draw near to him as long as he is set on evil, lest he overpower his friend [12].

12.7.0.en: e. We beware of him who is like a serpent that waits for the opportunity to bite charmers, or like a beast that devours him who approaches it [13].

12.7.1.en: f. We must not be deceived by the smile or tears of him who within desires to shed blood [15-16].

12.7.2.en: A friend is not known while you are in prosperity, nor does the enemy hide himself while you are in adversity [8].

12.7.3.en: In a man's prosperity his enemies grieve, and in his adversity even his friend departs from him [9].

12.7.4.en: Never trust your enemy, for as copper rusts so is his wickedness [10].

12.7.5.en: The enemy of good does not cease to oppose the children of God, using human beings or wicked angels to oppose them. Therefore Ben Sira warns us of these enemies, as instruments of iniquity who work for the kingdom of darkness.

12.7.6.en: The Christian is not a man isolated from society, but positive toward it, a servant of all and a lover of all. But he does not keep pace with the children of the world in their evil, that is, he does not practice love at the expense of the salvation of his soul or theirs. Therefore Holy Scripture demanded the necessity of care in choosing friends (Ps 1:1; 1 Cor 10:33; 1 Cor 5:6-7).

12.7.7.en: v Keeping company with those who are not wise shatters the heart, and conversation with the virtuous is a sweet spring.

12.7.8.en: v Do not stoop to the slack, or you will have made yourself of the lowest degree, but let your converse be with lovers of good, that your dwelling with them may be on high. Let your station be, with courage, in the places where the highest knowledge is. Go to the city of light, and do not go down to the sinners.

12.7.9.en: Mar Isaac the Syrian v This is the fuel of Satan who wrestles with us, who kindles the fire that burns us: corrupt talk with laymen... And the mother of evils is the throat and association with idle brethren. If our souls are stripped of this burning fuel, they will not fall into the snares of our wrestlers, and they can quickly fly to God, and through Him be delivered from the schemes of the devil.

12.7.10.en: The friendship of companions in idleness and amusement fills you with gluttony and evil. Oh, what unclean love and polluted act is this?! Flee, my brother, from those who are accustomed to this. Do not eat with them, and do not befriend them. Their table is unclean, and the demons are helpers in preparing it; the lovers of Christ the Bridegroom do not taste it. The banquet of the gluttonous man who is diverted by delicacies... defiles the soul of the meek, while a dry crust of bread from the table of the pure of soul cleanses it of all pains and defilements. The smell of the table of evil corrupts the intention of the pure, and the child is drawn to it like the dog to the butcher's house. And he who persists in prayer at all times, his table surpasses the fragrance of musk, and he who loves God longs for it like a treasure.

12.7.11.en: The Spiritual Elder v If someone loves me and I love him exceedingly, and I know that a lack has come upon me because of his love, I cut him off from me, and I cut myself off from him entirely.

12.7.12.en: Abba Agathon v If you have a friendship with one of the brethren and you suffer harm because of your association with him, hasten and cut yourself off from him. I do not say this to you, beloved, that you should hate people, no. But that you may cut off the causes of vice.

12.7.13.en: Mar Ephraim the Syrian v Hear what the Lord says: "Wherefore if thy hand or thy foot offend thee, cut them off, and cast them from thee: it is better for thee to enter into life halt or maimed, rather than having two hands or two feet to be cast into everlasting fire. And if thine eye offend thee, pluck it out, and cast it from thee: it is better for thee to enter into life with one eye, rather than having two eyes to be cast into hell fire" (Mt 18:8-9).

12.7.14.en: He did not say this about the members, but for the sake of the brethren and relatives who are to us in the position of necessary members... So he says that nothing is more harmful than bad company and wicked association, for friendship often harms or benefits... So He commands us with great plainness to cut off those who harm us...

12.7.15.en: He did not limit Himself to pronouncing woe on him through whom offenses come, but showed us the way by which a man is saved from offenses. What is this way? He said: Cut off the friendship of the wicked, even if it is in the forest... and do not gain them and destroy your soul with them.

12.7.16.en: St. John Chrysostom v I charge you, my son, not to walk on the road with a man from whom you have no spiritual benefit, lest you stumble on your journey. And do not keep company with an angry man or a hot-tempered one.

12.7.17.en: And do not associate with a slanderer or a talkative man.

12.7.18.en: Do not walk with the envious, for "the meek shall inherit the earth" (Mt 4:5).

12.7.19.en: Do not walk on the road with a slack man.

12.7.20.en: And do not befriend a confused man, nor one who has a friendship with a woman.

12.7.21.en: But watch yourself according to your strength that you have no friendship with a woman.

12.7.22.en: And do not walk on the road with one who is younger than you, lest you come to the rear.

12.7.23.en: St. Stephen of Thebes And even if he humbles himself and walks with bowed head, take heed to yourself and beware of him.

12.7.24.en: Be with him as one who polishes a mirror, and you will know that it is not spoiled forever [11].

12.7.25.en: v Do not spoil God's commandment for the sake of anyone's friendship. Do not return again to the city in which you sinned against God. Do not abandon worship, lest it become a snare and a stumbling block to you.

12.7.26.en: The blessed Abba Anthony Do not let him stand beside you, lest he throw you down and occupy your place.

12.7.27.en: Do not seat him at your right hand, lest he covet the seat of your honor, then you will understand my words at last, and be pricked with sorrow by my words [12].

12.7.28.en: St. Basil warns us against envy, because it offers an odious kind of friendship that does not know true love, rather all that occupies the friend is that he covets what his friend has, whether money or honor or privilege.

12.7.29.en: v There is no passion in the heart of man so corrupting as envy. Nothing harms a man like him who is afflicted with it. And as rust corrupts iron, so envy corrupts the man afflicted with it. Envy is a sorrow born of the neighbor's happiness. So the envious man is never without occasions for sorrow. Is the neighbor's field fertile? Is his house pleasant? Is he happy? All this drives the envious man to nurture his disease and to increase his torments. He is like a naked man at whose wound the arrows of everything are aimed. Is there someone strong and in good health? It is a blow that strikes the envious man. Is there a beautiful man? It is a new wound. Is a man intelligent, successful in his works, and doing good? All these are arrows that strike the envious man in the very core of his heart.

12.7.30.en: The hardest thing in this disease is that it is a shameful disease. The envious man complains of his condition and his strength declines, but if you ask him the cause of his illness, he is ashamed to confess it: "I am envious, and I feel bitterness in my heart, and I suffer from my friend's happiness. I cannot bear the success of others, and my neighbor's happiness seems to me a disaster." This is what he ought to say. But he prefers to say none of this, and to keep in the very depth of his heart his illness that wears him out.

12.7.31.en: There is no physician or medicine that heals this patient, for the only relief he awaits is the ruin of those he envies. And his hatred has only one object, which is to see his neighbor turn from happy to wretched. Then he gets up and shows friendship as soon as he finds him shedding tears. He does not know how to rejoice with those who rejoice, but only to weep with those who weep, and he is sorry for the calamity that has befallen, not out of a feeling of sympathy, but to increase the weight of the pain by reminding him of what was lost... Just as vultures hover over meadows and pleasant, fragrant places, and swoop down only on carcasses, so the envious man cannot stop at the splendor of a life and the greatness of the works accomplished, but sees in all of it only the blemishes. And if a mistake is made, which is hard to avoid in human undertakings, he publicizes it at once, and on it he bases the definition of every man, as if he were a caricaturist who sees in the portrait of a man only a deformed nose, or a hump on the back, or a natural or accidental defect in the face.

12.7.32.en: Moreover, he is an expert in deceptive distortions by which good can be mocked, and virtue defamed by means of the similar opposite. The courageous becomes the reckless, the wise the stupid, the just the hard-hearted, and the thrifty the miser. In a word, virtues are turned, in his view, into the vices that oppose them" [13].

12.7.33.en: St. Basil the Great Who will have pity on a charmer bitten by the serpent, or on all who go near wild beasts? [13]

12.8.0.en: v It is said: "Who will pity a charmer bitten by a serpent?" (see Sir 12:13) It is fitting for us to know his violent tyranny, so that we may flee from that slavery, and crush the dangerous longing for it. Someone says: "And how is that possible?" By introducing another longing, that is, the longing for heaven. For he who desires the Kingdom mocks the demon of greed and despises him. For he who becomes a slave of Christ no longer is a slave of greed, but its master [14].

12.9.0.en: 13 So he who keeps company with a sinful man is mingled with his sins. 14 He stays with you for an hour, and if you waver he does not stand firm. 15 The enemy shows sweetness with his lips, and in his heart he plots to throw you into the pit. 16 The enemy's eyes shed tears, and if he finds an opportunity he will not be satisfied with blood. 17 If evil befalls you, you will find him there before you, 18 and while he pretends to help you, he trips your foot. 19 He shakes his head and claps his hands, and whispers many things, and changes his countenance.

12.9.1.en: So no one pities him who keeps company with the sinful man and is entangled in his sins [14].

12.9.2.en: v As the fierce beast devours a tender and noble body unable to defend itself, so pride plants its violent fangs and pours into you its poison and its extremely foul smell. It tears off some parts after disfiguring them, and cuts off other parts and cuts them to pieces, and devours other parts. It throws the body to the ground, and hurls itself upon it with its eye on all its members. It attacks everyone who approaches the body, and does not leave it. Who can drive away this beast? (God), who permitted this battle, sends His angels when we beseech Him, and they break the beast's boldness, and bridle its mouth, and drive it away. But He intervenes in the battle on the condition that, when it is driven away, we do not return to it.

12.10.0.en: So after driving it away He commands it to remain far from us, if we, after we have been delivered from its young ones, which were driven off to their cave, still suffer from thousands of wounds and want to return to it and wake it and provoke it. Then He no longer has mercy on us and rescues us." "Who will pity a charmer bitten by a serpent, and all who go near wild beasts?" [15]

12.10.1.en: St. John Chrysostom He stays with you for a while, and if you stagger away from him he does not stand to support you [15].

12.10.2.en: The enemy speaks with sweetness on his lips, and in his heart he plans to throw you into the pit.

12.11.0.en: The enemy sheds tears, and if the opportunity arises, he is not satisfied with shedding your blood [16].

12.11.1.en: It is fitting for us to beware the wiles of the deceiving devil, who draws us to the wicked by their honeyed words, while in their heart they want to push us to destruction.

12.11.2.en: St. Cyril the Great warns us of the nets of the heretics who with their honeyed words corrupt the work of faith.

12.12.0.en: If evil befalls you, you find your enemy there before you, appearing to help you, and he trips your heel [17].

12.12.1.en: In rebuking the serpent, the Lord said to it: "He shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel" (Gen 3:15).

12.12.2.en: Behold the deceitful friend who bears the spirit of enmity: when he finds his friend in distress he hastens to him and appears jealous for him, wanting to rescue him, and behold, he trips his heel [17]. What does tripping his heel mean? If our Savior has granted us by the Cross to crush the head of the old serpent, the devil, behold this false friend trips his friend's heel so that he may not crush the head of Satan!

12.12.3.en: Faithful friendship, through which the Crucified One declares His dwelling in the two friends, so that they crush enmity and anger and deceit and guile, that is, all that belongs to the old serpent. The deceitful friend cannot bear the crushing of the head of his father the devil, therefore he trips his friend's heel.

12.13.0.en: He shakes his head, and claps his hands, and whispers many things, and changes his features [18].

12.13.1.en: The deceiving friend, when he sees his friend in distress, shakes his head and claps his hands and whispers... These outward movements are an expression of inner gloating (Ps 22:7; Job 16:4; Ezek 25:9).

12.13.2.en: This enemy does not stop at deceiving through the false smile or the lying tears, but hastens to add pains to the person's pains; he pushes him on and on toward destruction.

12.14.s.en: Grant me, O Lord, the spirit of discernment!

12.14.0.en: v I call upon You, O Lover of mankind, to grant me the spirit of discernment.

12.14.1.en: By Your grace I know how to offer kindness to my brethren, and to whom I offer it? And what are its limits?

12.14.2.en: All virtues without the spirit of discernment turn into vices.

12.14.3.en: My soul longs to offer You to them, for You are the satisfaction of hungry souls and the wealth of needy souls.

12.14.4.en: What good can I offer except the cleaving of all to You, O Maker of good things?!

12.14.5.en: Grant me to have compassion on sinners, as You have compassion on me, the sinner.

12.14.6.en: Grant me not to do good in ignorance and folly, lest by my kindness I push the wicked man on, and his evil is multiplied.

12.14.7.en: v Let me love sinners, and hate sin! You called Your betraying disciple Judas "Friend," yet You did not flatter him, but in firmness You said:

12.14.8.en: "Friend, betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss?"

12.14.9.en: Grant me not to flatter anyone, but in earnestness with tenderness to seek their salvation.

12.14.10.en: Let my friends be to me as a mirror.

12.14.11.en: I meet them, and so I realize my faults. And without deceit they discover their own faults.

12.14.12.en: v Let me imitate You who came down to us.

12.14.13.en: You took the last row of the rows of humanity.

12.14.14.en: You were crucified as a slave between two wicked thieves, whom society wanted to be rid of.

12.14.15.en: You were near them in the body; Your cross approaches their cross to within a few meters.

12.14.16.en: Dismas the thief believed in You as his Lord and King. He longed that You remember him in Your Kingdom, and You sent him at once to Paradise.

12.14.17.en: The heavenly ones were amazed that he gained the right of fellowship in the divine glories.

12.14.18.en: The other thief was at the same distance from Your cross in body.

12.14.19.en: But he was in a great chasm, for he surrendered himself to evil and rejected faith.

12.14.20.en: He became a son of the abyss, unable to meet You, depriving himself of enjoying Your majesty and Your glory!

12.14.21.en: The first thief gained boldness with You, opening his heart to You that You might establish Your Kingdom in it.

12.14.22.en: And the second bore a spirit of hatred of the truth, so he deprived his insight of seeing Your glories.

12.14.23.en: Grant me the grace of cleaving to You and to all Your true believers.

12.14.24.en: When shall I see You face to face?!
